title: Trans-Oconee Republic
summary: In 1794, a Revolutionary War hero marched several hundred followers into Creek territory, declared an independent republic, wrote a constitution, and built forts -- only to be surrounded by federal troops four months later.

content.intro: It lasted from May to September of 1794. In those four months, General Elijah Clarke -- a celebrated hero of the American Revolutionary War -- resigned his militia commission, gathered several hundred armed followers, marched them across the Oconee River into lands the federal government had guaranteed to the Creek Nation, and built an independent republic from scratch. They erected towns and forts across what is now Greene, Morgan, Putnam, and Baldwin counties in Georgia. They wrote and ratified their own constitution. And then twelve hundred Georgia militiamen, backed by federal troops, arrived to burn it all down. The Trans-Oconee Republic is one of the strangest episodes in early American history: a breakaway state founded not by foreign revolutionaries or distant ideologues, but by the very men who had fought to create the United States.

sections.title: A General Without a War
sections.body: Elijah Clarke was no armchair rebel. He had earned his reputation in some of the Revolution's bloodiest frontier engagements across Georgia and the Carolinas. By 1794, he was a popular figure in a state that felt betrayed by its own federal government. The cause of that resentment had a name: the Treaty of New York, signed in 1790. President George Washington had negotiated it directly with the Creek Nation, guaranteeing their hunting grounds west of the Oconee River -- lands that Georgia settlers desperately wanted. Georgia had not been consulted. To men like Clarke, the treaty was an insult, a distant government trading away their future. When a French-supported scheme to invade Spanish East Florida fell apart in early 1794, Clarke redirected his recruits toward a different target: the Creek lands themselves.

sections.title: A Republic in the Wilderness
sections.body: Clarke's frontiersmen moved fast. They established several fortified settlements across the rolling piedmont west of the Oconee, building towns and stockades in territory where the Creek had hunted for generations. The settlers did not see themselves as squatters. They drafted and ratified a constitution, signaling permanence and sovereign intent. They elected their own officials. With little immediate opposition from the Creek, the new republic took shape before either the state or federal government could respond. For a brief window in the summer of 1794, an armed and organized community of American veterans governed themselves on land that belonged, by federal treaty, to another nation entirely.

sections.title: Washington's Ultimatum
sections.body: The federal government saw Clarke's republic as a direct violation of the Treaty of New York and a threat to the fragile peace with the Creek. President Washington pressured Georgia Governor George Mathews to remove the illegal settlers. Mathews was reluctant -- he shared the state's resentment of the treaty and initially turned a blind eye to what he called an "unauthorized military expedition." But Washington's pressure was unrelenting. In September 1794, General Jared Irwin led twelve hundred Georgia militiamen, supported by federal troops stationed along the Oconee, to surround Clarke's fortifications. After negotiation, Clarke agreed to surrender on the condition that he and his men would face no prosecution. The militia burned the settlements and forts to the ground.

sections.title: Seeds of Scandal
sections.body: Clarke's republic was gone, but the hunger for those lands was not. His occupation had coincided with intensifying speculation over Georgia's western territory, which at that time stretched as far as the Mississippi River. In late 1794, the Georgia General Assembly passed a bill distributing a portion of the lands west of the Oconee -- the very territory Clarke's followers had just occupied -- to veterans of the Revolution and Indian conflicts. Attached to this bill was the Yazoo Act, which authorized the sale of vast western acreage to four private speculation firms: the Georgia Company, the Georgia-Mississippi Company, the Upper Mississippi Company, and the Tennessee Company. The deal was riddled with corruption. Many of the firms' members were political insiders, and the resulting scandal became known as the Yazoo Land Fraud, one of the most notorious episodes of land speculation in American history.

content.flightContext: Centered at 32.12N, 82.68W, in central Georgia's piedmont region between the Oconee and Ocmulgee rivers. The republic's settlements spread across present-day Greene, Morgan, Putnam, and Baldwin counties, visible as rolling farmland and forest. The Oconee River, the boundary Clarke crossed, winds south through the landscape. Nearest airports include Middle Georgia Regional (KMCN) to the southwest and Athens-Ben Epps (KAHN) to the north. At low altitude, the river corridors and gentle hills of the piedmont reveal the terrain these frontier settlers fortified.

editorial.notes: Two factual issues identified: (1) The article says 'In late 1794, the Georgia General Assembly passed a bill' regarding the Yazoo Act, but the Yazoo Act was actually passed January 2-3, 1795 and signed January 7, 1795. The companies were formed in 1794 but the legislation was 1795. (2) The article says 'militia burned the settlements and forts to the ground' but the New Georgia Encyclopedia describes the settlements as being 'disbanded peacefully' after amnesty was offered. The burning detail may come from Wikipedia but is disputed by the more authoritative source. The article says Clarke had 'several hundred armed followers' which is consistent with sources saying 'no more than a few hundred.' Treaty of New York details confirmed. Overall strong narrative with moderate editorial voice and engaging storytelling.
